name: The Impression

CREATORS.summary: Two creator populations ran side by side and neither owned the web outright. Traditional agencies, by now inside four holding companies, still made the ads that carried most of the money — but their pay model was collapsing mid-era. Among large US national advertisers the share paying a media commission fell from 61% in 1994 toward 10% by 2003, and Census data show agency income from commissions and markups sliding from 70% of the industry's take in 1992 to 59% in 1997, with the realized commission rate down to about 11%. Web creative went instead to a new class of interactive shops — Razorfish, Organic, Agency.com, iXL, Scient, USWeb/CKS — that sold strategy and build together, floated on dot-com equity, then died with it: marchFIRST (Whittman-Hart plus USWeb/CKS, formed 1 March 2000) lost $437M in a single quarter and filed Chapter 11 on 13 April 2001. Creative itself was severely constrained: from December 1996 the IAB and CASIE published eight voluntary banner sizes, and the 468x60 full banner under a hard file-size budget became the era's unit of authorship. A third creator class appeared at the very end and had no agency at all: on GoTo/Overture and on Google's AdWords, the advertiser typed its own listing into a web form, and an editorial reviewer, not an art director, decided whether it ran.

BUYERS.summary: The buyer of a web ad in this era was, disproportionately, another internet company spending venture or IPO money. DoubleClick reported that traditional advertisers only passed half of its network revenue in the fourth quarter of 2000 — meaning internet firms had been the majority of demand until then — and Yahoo blamed its 44% marketing-services collapse in 2001 directly on internet companies losing access to capital markets. Across all media the buyer mix barely moved: national brand money was about 42% of the $247.5B US market in 2000, local retail about 31%, direct-response (direct mail plus directories plus online performance deals) about 19%, and classified about 8%. Almost none of the local or classified money was online yet: online classifieds were 7% of a $8.2B internet market in 2000, i.e. under 3% of the $20.2B US classified pool. The era's genuinely new buyer class was the self-serve advertiser with no agency: Google signed roughly 350 businesses in AdWords' first month (October 2000), and by December 2001 Overture had about 53,000 paying advertisers, mostly small merchants who had never bought media through an agency at all. That buyer class is era 6's engine; here it is still a rounding error.

claims.statement: Advertising customers on Yahoo's online properties in 1998 (up from approximately 2,600 in 1997 and 700 in 1996) - the biggest web seller's entire advertiser base was in the low thousands. In the single quarter ended 30 September 1998 the count was about 1,950.

national_brand.statement: US national-brand advertisers' measured media spend in 2000 (Coen national total less direct mail, national Yellow Pages and performance-priced internet). These buyers supplied most of the $8.2B internet market — IAB's FY2000 advertiser mix was consumer 31%, computing 18%, financial services 14%, business services 9%, media 8% — but the web was still under 8% of their own budgets.

national_brand.method: Coen/McCann 'Total National' 2000 = $151.664B. The four money-type pools sum exactly to the $247.472B Coen grand total by construction. SELLERS.summary: Web inventory concentrated faster than any earlier medium. The ten largest online ad sellers took 71% of US internet ad revenue in the fourth quarter of 2000 and 77% a year later; the top 25 took 91% and the top 50 took 98%. Those sellers were portals — search engines and portals alone accounted for 36% of revenue by content genre in 2000 — and their business was a magazine business with a server: Yahoo booked $1,110M of net revenue in 2000, of which $968M was banners and sponsorships, at an 86.5% gross margin. Between the portal and the advertiser sat a second layer that took a real cut: DoubleClick's network arm ran a 25-40% gross margin, meaning publishers kept roughly 60-75% of network-sold money, while its ad-serving arm charged separately and served 621 billion ads worldwide in 2000. In paid search the intermediary cut was far larger and pointed the other way: Overture paid out 56% of 2001 revenue as traffic acquisition cost to the portals and browsers that sent it queries, because more than 95% of its traffic came from affiliates. The shakeout was brutal and fast — Excite@Home filed Chapter 11 on 1 October 2001, and Yahoo's revenue fell 35% in a single year.

MEDIUM.summary: The era's headline is not that the web arrived but that it barely dented the ranking. Newspapers were the largest single US medium every year from 1994 through 2000, peaking at $49.05B; direct mail then overtook them in 2001 ($44.7B against $44.3B) and stayed ahead. Yellow Pages, the structural ancestor of paid search, grew right through the web's arrival, from $9.8B in 1994 to $13.2B in 2000. Newspaper classified peaked at $19.6B in 2000, about 40% of newspaper advertising revenue, with recruitment alone at $8.7B. Against those, the internet reached somewhere between 2.6% and 3.7% of US ad spend in 2000 depending on whose internet number and whose denominator you use, then shrank in 2001. Two definitional cautions matter inside this window: the Coen series has no internet line at all before 1997, so 1994-1996 web spend is reconstruction, not data; and 'Out of Home' replaced 'Billboards' as a Coen category in 2000 at roughly three times the expenditure ($4.78B against $1.73B on the 1999 overlap), an artefact that will look like a real jump on any chart that does not annotate it.

claims.method: Basis must be declared, not blended. Upper bound 3.7 is the IAB's own published share, which implies a denominator near $222B rather than Coen's $247.5B. The three are not averaged; the interval spans them.

SCALE.summary: US measured advertising grew from $153.0B in 1994 to $247.5B in 2000, the largest run in the series' post-war history, then fell 6.5% to $231.3B in 2001 — one of only six down years in seventy (the others being 1938, 1942, 1961 and 1991). Advertising's share of GDP peaked in 2000 at roughly 2.3-2.5% depending on the series and the GDP vintage, and has never regained that level, which makes 2000 the high-water mark of advertising intensity in the American economy and complicates any story in which the web enlarged the pie. Internet advertising itself went from unmeasurable in 1994-1995 to $267M in 1996, $8.1-8.2B in 2000 and back to $7.1-7.2B in 2001, with four consecutive quarterly declines from the Q4 2000 peak of $2.16B. By money type in 2000 the market split roughly $103.6B national brand, $76.2B local retail, $47.5B direct response and $20.2B classified — and the two pools search would later take, classified and direct response, were together worth $67.7B while the entire internet ad market was worth $8.2B.

claims.statement: Total US measured advertising expenditure in 1994, the first year of the era.

sources.name: Coen Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset (McCann-Erickson series, curated by Douglas Galbi), 14 September 2008 revision

Either way 2001 was only the fifth annual decline in the Coen series since 1934 (1938, 1942, 1961, 1991, 2001); across the full 1919-2007 series there are eleven, the others clustered in 1921 and 1930-1933.

claims.statement: Worldwide major-media advertising expenditure in 2000, the era's global peak. Zenith Media's series put global adspend at $289B actual for 1998 with $320B and $339B projected for 1999 and 2000; WARC's series records a 3.1% global decline in 2001.

Zenith's published forecast of $339B for 2000 is taken as the upper anchor and discounted slightly because it was made ex ante and the year came in weaker than forecast in the second half; the WARC-recorded -3.1% global decline in 2001 implies a 2001 level near $325B on the same basis. The lower bound is NOT justifiable from the US Coen total, which is an all-media measure including direct mail and directories and is not comparable to Zenith's major-media basis (the comparable US major-media figure for 2000 is roughly $150B). The bound instead reflects the spread between Zenith's ex-ante $339B forecast and the weaker outturn implied by the WARC-recorded -3.1% global decline in 2001.

PRICING.summary: The web's founding pricing decision was to copy the magazine. HotWired priced its October 1994 launch sponsorships at $30,000 for twelve weeks because a page in Wired cost about $10,000 a month, and the industry then generalised that into the CPM: 43% of US internet ad revenue was priced purely per thousand impressions in 2000, and another 47% on hybrid deals that started from a CPM. Rate cards behaved like magazine rate cards too — around $37 CPM for an average banner in December 1997, still $25 for a full banner in Q4 2000 — but realised prices did not, because unsold inventory diluted everything. Portal 'anchor tenancy' deals rebuilt the sponsorship logic of 1930s radio: Excite paid Netscape $5.0M for each of two Premier Provider slots in 1996 and a minimum $8.25M in 1997. Against all of this, GoTo.com from June 1998 sold a completely different thing: not an impression but a click, ranked purely by bid, paid at the bid, minimum five cents, with the advertiser setting the price. Overture's average realised price per click was $0.23 in Q4 2001. Google's answer in October 2000 was still a CPM — AdWords launched with fixed $15, $12 and $10 CPM tiers — which is exactly why era 6 begins where it does.

claims.statement: Share of US internet advertising revenue priced on a pure CPM or impression basis in 2000, with 47% on hybrid impression-plus-performance deals and only 10% on pure performance. By 2001 the split was 48% CPM, 40% hybrid, 12% performance — the impression, not the click, was the era's unit of trade.
claims.unit: percent of US internet ad revenue priced per impression

MEASUREMENT.summary: This is the first era in which the seller counted the audience with its own instrument and the buyer had no third-party audit to appeal to. The counting technology was the ad server: DoubleClick's DART delivered 621 billion ads worldwide in 2000 and its log was the invoice. Two rival counting institutions grew up beside it — server-side log auditors (I/PRO, NetCount, ABC Interactive) and user-panel meters (Media Metrix, RelevantKnowledge, then Nielsen//NetRatings from 1998) — and they disagreed, because proxy caching hid impressions from server logs while panels missed work and school access. Standard-setting was industry-funded and voluntary: the IAB and CASIE published eight banner sizes on 10 December 1996, and Procter & Gamble convened about 200 industry leaders at the FAST summit in Cincinnati in August 1998 precisely because only 16% of marketers said they were satisfied with online ad measurement. The number the whole market watched, the click-through rate, fell from double digits at HotWired's launch to roughly 0.3% by 2000 — a fall in the very metric that had justified the medium's premium CPMs, and the reason a pay-per-click seller could credibly attack the impression.

claims.statement: Average banner click-through rate by mid-2000, quoted by Overture in its own 10-K (attributed to eMarketer) as the failure of impression-based advertising; the IAB reported the same 0.3% with business-to-business advertisers nearer 0.5%. Launch-era rates in 1994-96 were reported in the mid-single digits to double digits, all self-reported.

TARGETING.summary: Targeting in this era ran on two incompatible logics, and the losing one was the more advanced. The dominant logic was profile-based: DoubleClick's DART used cookies to target by site, domain, geography, browser, time of day and frequency cap across a network reaching 48% of the US internet audience, and in 1999 DoubleClick bought Abacus, whose direct-mail cooperative database covered purchase histories on roughly 90% of US households. Merging the two would have given the web named-person targeting; EPIC's FTC complaint of 10 February 2000 and the resulting investigation forced DoubleClick to abandon the plan on 2 March 2000, and the first great privacy retreat of the ad-tech era happened before third-party behavioural targeting ever really shipped. The other logic was intent: GoTo/Overture matched the advertisement to the words the user had just typed, which needed no profile at all and no cookie. It was tiny — keyword search was 1% of US internet ad revenue in 2000 — but it delivered 442 million clicks in Q4 2001 alone, and Overture's own filing sized the opportunity against Yellow Pages calls and direct-mail responses rather than against banner impressions.

claims.statement: Share of US households covered by the Abacus cooperative purchase database that DoubleClick acquired in 1999 — the asset that would have converted anonymous cookie profiles into named-person targeting.

sources.name: In re DoubleClick Inc. Privacy Litigation, 154 F. Supp. 2d 497 (S.D.N.Y. 2001), background section

Network reach, not publisher relationships, was what made cookie-based targeting economically meaningful.

events.title: HotWired launches the web's first paid banner campaign
events.desc: Wired's HotWired went live with banner advertising from about a dozen brands simultaneously — AT&T, MCI, Volvo, Club Med, Sprint, IBM, Zima among them — sold by Rick Boyce at roughly $30,000 for a twelve-week sponsorship, a price set by analogy to a $10,000 page in the print magazine. There was no single 'first banner ad': a dozen went live at once, GNN had sold a clickable ad to the law firm Heller Ehrman in 1993, and Prodigy carried screen ads years earlier. The famous 44% click-through figure is self-reported and unaudited; participants in Digiday's oral history recall 15%. Treat the superlative as attributed legend and the launch itself as the datable event.

claim.statement: Brands live with banner advertising on HotWired at launch on 27 October 1994. Digiday's oral history counts twelve; other accounts say fourteen signed advertisers.

sources.name: Digiday, 'The beginning of a giant industry: an oral history of the first banner ad'
Campaign, 'No 73: The first banner ad' (12 advertisers; $30,000 for 12 weeks each)
Fast Company, 'The Trailblazing, Candy-Colored History Of The Online Banner Ad' (GNN 1993, Prodigy, no single first)

events.title: IAB and CASIE publish the first voluntary banner standards
events.desc: The Internet Advertising Bureau, founded earlier in 1996, and CASIE jointly issued a 'Proposal for Voluntary Model Banner Sizes' naming the eight most common web ad units, including the 468x60 full banner. Standardising the unit is what made an impression tradable across publishers, which is what made a CPM market possible — the same function audited circulation performed for print in 1914.

claim.statement: Voluntary standard banner sizes published jointly by the IAB and CASIE on 10 December 1996.

sources.name: IAB press release, 10 December 1996

events.title: GoTo.com launches the pure-bid keyword auction
events.desc: Bill Gross's GoTo.com, announced in February 1998 and live on 1 June 1998, sold search placement by open auction: advertisers bid per click, listings ranked in descending order of bid, and the winner paid its own bid. Human editors reviewed every listing. It made $822,000 in 1998 and $288.1M in 2001. This is the mechanism era 6 inherits and modifies: Google's contribution is quality weighting and next-price billing, not the auction itself.

claim.statement: GoTo.com revenue in 1998, its launch year (rising to $26.8M in 1999, $103.1M in 2000 and $288.1M in 2001).

sources.name: Overture Services, Inc. (formerly GoTo.com), Form 10-K for FY2001, Selected Financial Data, SEC EDGAR

events.title: Procter & Gamble convenes the FAST summit
events.desc: P&G invited roughly 200 leaders from agencies, media, associations and advertisers to Cincinnati for the Future of Advertising Stakeholders summit, aimed at fixing the web's measurement, format and buying plumbing so that large brand advertisers could spend at scale. It produced voluntary guidelines on ad models, creative formats, ad-impression measurement, a standard insertion order and a standard reporting template. The organisation dissolved in 2001; most of its questions were still open when it did.

events.title: DoubleClick completes the Abacus merger
events.desc: DoubleClick completed its acquisition of Abacus Direct, whose direct-mail cooperative database held purchase histories on roughly 90% of US households, and quietly removed the promise that its cookie data would not be joined to personally identifiable information. EPIC complained to the FTC on 10 February 2000; the FTC opened an investigation; on 2 March 2000 chief executive Kevin O'Connor called the plan a mistake and shelved it. The web's first attempt at identity-resolved targeting was killed before it launched.

events.title: AOL and Time Warner announce their merger
events.desc: AOL agreed to acquire Time Warner in a deal valued at roughly $162-182 billion depending on the measure — the moment an advertising-and-subscription internet portal was worth more than the largest media company in the world. It marks the top of the ad-funded portal's valuation and, in retrospect, the top of the impression era's confidence.

claim.statement: Announced value of the AOL-Time Warner merger, 10 January 2000. Contemporaneous and retrospective figures differ by the treatment of debt and the stock price used: ABC News reports $162B; History.com reports $182B in stock and debt for a combined entity valued near $350B; $165B is the figure most commonly cited in retrospective accounts for the announced equity value.

sources.name: History.com, 'AOL-Time Warner merger announced, January 10, 2000'
ABC News, 'AOL Buys Time Warner for $162 billion'

events.title: The dot-com Super Bowl
events.desc: Super Bowl XXXIV carried a record number of internet-company advertisements — 14 dot-com companies in-game, 21 dot-com ads all told, close to 20% of the 61 spots available — at an average of about $2.2 million for thirty seconds. It is the clearest single demonstration that the web's advertising boom was funded by venture and IPO capital being spent on television, not by the web's own economics.

claim.statement: Dot-com companies running in-game advertisements in Super Bowl XXXIV, 30 January 2000, at an average of roughly $2.2M per 30-second spot. Counts vary by definition: 14 pure dot-com companies ran in-game spots; including five pre-bubble companies running tech-related ads and two pre-game ads gives 21 dot-com ads in total, close to 20% of the 61 spots available, for about $44M of advertising.

sources.name: Wikipedia, 'Dot-com commercials during Super Bowl XXXIV'
Fast Company, '20 years ago, the dot-coms took over the Super Bowl'

events.title: Google launches AdWords as a CPM product
events.desc: Google opened AdWords to self-serve signups with about 350 businesses and agencies, selling short text ads beside the search results at fixed rates of $15, $12 and $10 per thousand impressions by position. It was an extension of the CPM 'premium sponsorship' programme announced that August. Google priced the impression for another sixteen months; the auction arrives with AdWords Select in February 2002, which is where era 6 begins.

claim.statement: Top-position CPM at the AdWords general-availability announcement of 23 October 2000 ($12 middle, $10 bottom), by which point roughly 350 businesses and agencies worldwide had already adopted the product during its beta earlier that month.

sources.name: Google press release, 'Google Launches Self-Service Advertising Program', 23 October 2000

events.title: Excite@Home files for Chapter 11 as the portal model breaks
events.desc: Excite@Home, formed by a $6.7 billion merger and once worth about $35 billion, filed for Chapter 11 on 1 October 2001 and agreed to sell its network to AT&T for $307 million. In the same month GoTo.com renamed itself Overture Services. The two events together are the era's hinge: the impression-selling portal failed while the click-selling auction survived and grew through the same downturn.

events.title: The crash resets the market
events.desc: US internet advertising revenue fell about 12% for the year to $7.1-7.2 billion after four consecutive quarterly declines, and total US measured advertising fell 6.5% to $231.3 billion — one of only six down years in seventy. Banners fell from 48% to 36% of internet revenue, barter rose from 6% to 10%, seller concentration rose to 77% for the top ten, and performance-priced deals rose from 10% to 12%. Impression pricing survived the crash smaller; performance pricing came out of it larger.

claim.statement: Decline in US internet advertising revenue in 2001 — the medium's first ever down year, against a 6.5% fall in total US measured ad spend.

sources.name: IAB / PricewaterhouseCoopers, Internet Advertising Revenue Report, 2001 Full-Year Results (June 2002), p. 6
IAB press release, 'Internet Advertising Revenue Totaled $1.7 Billion for Q4 2001'

revenue_per_unit.statement: Effective revenue per delivered US web ad impression in 2000, the era's peak year — about $7 per thousand, against rate cards of $25-$35 per thousand for a full banner. The gap is unsold inventory, volume discounting, house ads and barter, exactly as DoubleClick described it: 'increases in the amounts of unsold inventory, which diluted the effective price of delivered advertising impressions.'
revenue_per_unit.method: Numerator: impression-priced US internet ad revenue in 2000 = banners (48%) plus sponsorships (28%) of IAB/PwC FY2000 revenue $8.225B = $6.25B. Denominator: US delivered display impressions in 2000, triangulated three ways. (1) AdRelevance measured 172 billion US impressions in Q4 2000 and 65 billion in December 2000; with Q4 the seasonal peak at roughly 28-30% of the year, that implies 575-615 billion for 2000, and AdRelevance's monitoring method undercounts unmeasured sites, so treat it as a floor. (2) DoubleClick's DART served 621 billion ads worldwide in 2000 for 2,000+ clients; DART was the largest but far from the only ad server (Yahoo, AOL and MSN ran their own; AdForce, Engage and 24/7 competed), so if DART was 25-40% of worldwide served ads the worldwide total was 1.6-2.5 trillion and the US share roughly half of that. (3) Yahoo alone delivered about 784 million page views per day ex-Japan in December 2000, roughly 24 billion in the month. Taking the three together, US delivered display impressions in 2000 were between 0.6 and 1.5 trillion, central 0.9 trillion. $6.25B / 0.9T = $0.0069 per impression. Cross-check: Yahoo's marketing-services revenue of $968.3M over an estimated 222 billion ex-Japan page views for 2000 (linear interpolation between 431M/day ex-Japan in December 1999 and 784M/day ex-Japan in December 2000) gives $4.37 per thousand page views, in the same band. CI reflects the impression-count uncertainty, which dominates.

sources.name: IAB / PricewaterhouseCoopers, Internet Advertising Revenue Report, 2001 Full-Year Results (revenue and format split)
AdRelevance / Jupiter Media Metrix Q4 2000 impression counts via Encyclopedia.com, 'Internet Advertising'
DoubleClick Inc., Form 10-K for FY2000 (621 billion DART ads served worldwide in 2000; unsold-inventory dilution language in MD&A)
Yahoo! Inc., Form 10-K for FY2001 (page views per day; marketing services revenue)

cost_to_serve.statement: Direct cost of serving one web ad impression in 2000 — roughly $0.90 per thousand at portal scale, comprising content, bandwidth and equipment depreciation (about $0.68 per thousand page views at Yahoo) plus ad-delivery infrastructure (about $0.09 per thousand ads at DoubleClick). Marginal cost was trivially small; the era's real cost was the human ad sales force, which Yahoo carried at 38% of revenue.
cost_to_serve.method: Two audited anchors, summed. (a) Ad-delivery infrastructure: DoubleClick TechSolutions FY2000 revenue $203.4M at 71.6% gross margin implies cost of ad delivery (internet access, ad-delivery system depreciation, facilities, operating personnel) of $57.8M against 621 billion ads served = $0.000093 per ad, i.e. $0.093 per thousand. (b) Publisher content and bandwidth: Yahoo FY2000 cost of revenues $149.744M (third-party content fees, internet connection charges, equipment depreciation, production) against an estimated 222 billion ex-Japan page views for 2000 (linear interpolation between 431M/day ex-Japan in December 1999 and 784M/day ex-Japan in December 2000) = $0.675 per thousand page views. Sum at portal scale ~$0.77 per thousand impressions; central raised to $0.90 because smaller publishers ran materially worse infrastructure economics than Yahoo. CI upper bound of $2.50 per thousand covers content-heavy publishers; lower bound covers pure-network sellers with no content cost.

sources.name: DoubleClick Inc., Form 10-K for FY2000 (TechSolutions revenue $203.4M, gross margin 71.6%, 621 billion ads served; cost-of-revenue definition)
Yahoo! Inc., Form 10-K for FY2001 (cost of revenues $149.744M in 2000 and $157.001M in 2001; page views per day; sales and marketing 38% of 2000 revenue)

margin.statement: Gross margin on a web ad impression at the seller in 2000 — Yahoo's audited figure was 86.5% and fell to 78.1% in 2001. The number that matters is the contrast: gross margins were print-beating while operating results were catastrophic, because selling an impression cost far more than serving it. Yahoo spent 38% of 2000 revenue on sales and marketing and still lost $92.8M in 2001; ad networks made only 25-40% gross margin because they paid the publisher out of the same impression.
margin.method: Anchored on Yahoo's audited FY2000 accounts: net revenues $1,110.178M less cost of revenues $149.744M = 86.5% gross margin (78.1% in 2001 on $717.422M and $157.001M). Cross-checked bottom-up against the unit figures above: (0.0070 - 0.0009) / 0.0070 = 87%. Central set slightly below Yahoo at 85% because the market-wide mix includes ad networks, whose gross margin was 25.3% in 2000 (32.6% excluding a one-off write-off) since publisher payouts sit in their cost of revenue. CI lower bound of 70% reflects that network-intermediated share.

sources.name: Yahoo! Inc., Form 10-K for FY2001 (net revenues and cost of revenues, FY1999-FY2001; net loss $92.8M in 2001)
DoubleClick Inc., Form 10-K for FY2000 (DoubleClick Media gross margin 25.3% in 2000, 32.6% ex-writeoff, 39.8% in 1999, 21.2% in 1998)

boundary_notes:
Shared with era 4 (1976-1993, Segmentation): the Coen/McCann series total for 1993 is $140.956B, rising to $153.024B in 1994, so era 4 should close on 1993 and era 5 open on 1994 with no gap. Direct mail was $27.266B in 1993 and Yellow Pages $9.517B; both grew through the whole of era 5. Newspapers were the largest single US medium at the end of era 4 ($32.025B in 1993) and remained so until 2000, so neither era should claim a medium crossover at the 1993/94 boundary. Agency compensation: 61% of large national advertisers still paid commissions in 1994, so era 4 owns the start of the commission's decline (71% in 1982) and era 5 owns its middle.

Shared with era 6 (2002-2008, The Auction): era 5 ends with the mechanism in place but not yet dominant. As of December 2001 Overture ran a pure first-price, pure-bid auction with a $0.05 minimum bid, human editorial review, ~53,000 advertisers, 442 million paid introductions in the quarter, an average realised price of $0.23 per click, and traffic acquisition costs of 56% of revenue. Overture's FY2001 revenue was $288.133M; Google's total FY2001 revenue was $86.4M. Era 6 therefore inherits Overture as the paid-search revenue leader, consistent with the pre-cleared constraint that Overture led through 2002 ($667.7M FY2002). AdWords existed from 23 October 2000 as a fixed-CPM self-serve product at $15/$12/$10 per thousand impressions; the auction (AdWords Select) is a February 2002 event and belongs to era 6, as does the AOL syndication flip of May 2002, the April 2004 trademark-keyword policy change, and the 2004 Overture patent settlement (~2.7M shares, ~$230M). Era 6 also inherits the pools search will take: US classified peaked at $19.6B in 2000 (about 40% of newspaper ad revenue, recruitment $8.7B) and Yellow Pages was $13.228B in 2000 and still rising, while total US internet advertising was only $7.1-8.2B. The internet ad market handed to era 6 is $7.1-7.2B for 2001 (IAB/PwC), 48% CPM-priced, 40% hybrid, 12% performance, with the top ten sellers holding 77%. Total US measured ad spend handed over is $231.287B for 2001 (Coen), having peaked at $247.472B in 2000 at roughly 2.4% of GDP — a peak share never regained, which means era 6's growth story must be told as reallocation, not expansion.

Series and definition warnings that both neighbours must carry: (1) the Coen series has no internet line before 1997, so 1994-1996 web spend is reconstruction; (2) 'Out of Home' replaced 'Billboards' as a Coen category in 2000 at roughly 2.8x the expenditure on the 1999 overlap year; (3) Coen is bottom-up advertiser billings at list prices while IAB/PwC is top-down seller revenue, which is why Coen's internet line ($6.507B in 2000) sits about 20% below IAB's ($8.087-8.225B) and the two must never be mixed inside one line.
